## 1. Decide what you want to estimate

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Task:** estimate the number of living juniper trees in a mapped area.

\vspace{1em}

- Agree what counts as a tree: species, minimum size, etc.
- Draw the survey boundary before selecting plots.
- Choose the survey dates and obtain access permission.
- State which area the final estimate will describe.


:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\fill[grn!10] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[<->] (0,-0.3)--node[below,font=\small]{50 m}(5,-0.3);
\draw[<->] (-0.3,0)--node[left,font=\small,rotate=90]{50 m}(-0.3,5);
\node[align=center] at (2.5,2.5) {Training patch\\$A=2{,}500$ m$^2$\\$=0.25$ ha};
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-1.3) {Define the area first};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 2. Choose a plot size that you can count completely

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Simple option: fixed-size square plots.**

\vspace{1em}

- Use $10\times10$ m squares for this training exercise.
- Mark corners using a tape and compass.
- Search each plot in adjacent lanes so trees are counted once.
- Agree what to do at boundaries e.g. include north/east edges, exclude south/west edges.

\vspace{1em}

Use the stem base to decide whether a tree is inside. Measure horizontal distances on slopes.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=Stealth]
\fill[grn!8] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[rd,dashed,thick] (0,5)--(0,0)--(5,0);
\draw[bl,very thick] (0,5)--(5,5)--(5,0);
\draw[bl!60,->,thick] (0.5,0.3)--(0.5,4.6)--(1.5,4.6)--(1.5,0.4)--(2.5,0.4)--(2.5,4.6)--(3.5,4.6)--(3.5,0.4)--(4.5,0.4)--(4.5,4.6);
\foreach \x/\y in {0.8/2.7,2.2/3.4,3.6/1.8}{\fill[grn!70!black] (\x,\y) circle (0.09);}
\node[above,font=\small] at (2.5,5) {North: include};
\node[below,font=\small] at (2.5,0) {South: exclude};
\node[font=\small] at (2.5,-0.85) {$10\times10$ m $=100$ m$^2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 3. Make a complete list of possible plots

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Divide the training patch into **equal, non-overlapping squares**.

\vspace{1em}

- Give each square a unique ID, 1--25.
- Save its corners or centre as GPS coordinates.
- Include open areas as well as dense juniper stands.
- In a real landscape, decide how to handle boundary plots before sampling.

\vspace{1em}

The calculation later assumes equal-area plots that cover the entire target area.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\surveygrid\plotnumbers
\draw[<->] (0,-0.3)--node[below,font=\small]{50 m}(5,-0.3);
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-1.3) {Every square can be selected};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 4. Option A: select plots at random

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Simple random sampling** is often a simple, effective approach.

\vspace{1em}

- Put all 25 plot IDs into a bag, mix well and draw five without replacement.
- Or use a computer random-number generator.
- Save the selected list.
- Visit those plots, including empty-looking ones.
- Plan an efficient route after selecting the plots.

\vspace{1em}

Here the selected IDs are **4, 6, 12, 14 and 21**. Use a pilot study or power analysis to determine number of plots.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\sampleplots\surveygrid\plotnumbers
\node[font=\small,text=bl] at (2.5,-0.45) {Blue = selected plots};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 5. Option B: sample separately within habitats

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Use **stratified random sampling** when mapped habitats differ.

- Draw habitat boundaries before seeing the counts.
- Make a plot list for each habitat; select randomly within each list.
- Start with effort proportional to habitat area.
- Keep the habitat label with every count.

Estimate each habitat total, then add:
$$\hat N=\frac{n_1}{p_{c,1}}+\frac{n_2}{p_{c,2}}.$$
Here $n_h$ is the tree count and $p_{c,h}$ the fraction of habitat $h$ surveyed.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\fill[grn!22] (0,2) rectangle (5,5);
\fill[orange!15] (0,0) rectangle (5,2);
\foreach \x/\y in {0/4,3/4,1/3,4/3,0/2,3/2,1/1,4/1,0/0,3/0}{\fill[bl!65] (\x,\y) rectangle +(1,1);}
\surveygrid
\draw[very thick] (0,2)--(5,2);
\node[above,font=\small] at (2.5,5) {Woodland: 60\% of area};
\node[below,font=\small] at (2.5,0) {Open slope: 40\% of area};
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-0.95) {Example: 6 woodland + 4 open plots};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 6. Option C: use a grid with a random start

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Systematic sampling** spreads effort across the area.

\vspace{1em}

- Choose the spacing before going to the field.
- Randomly choose the grid's starting offset in both directions.
- Here, use every second row and column of the plot grid.
- Check that the pattern does not repeatedly follow roads or habitat bands.

\vspace{1em}

Selected IDs: **1, 3, 5, 11, 13, 15, 21, 23, 25**.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\fill[bl!14] (0,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (2,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (2,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (4,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (4,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (0,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (2,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (2,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (4,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (4,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (0,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (2,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (2,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (4,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (4,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\surveygrid\plotnumbers
\node[font=\small,text=bl] at (2.5,-0.55) {Every second row and column};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 7. Run a pilot beforehand (optional)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Test the method in a small sample spanning the main conditions.

\vspace{1em}

- Time travel, plot marking, counting and data entry.
- Check whether two observers apply the same counting rules.
- Inspect variation in counts and missed trees.
- Use those results to set plot size and the number of plots needed for useful precision.

\vspace{1em}

If the protocol changes, keep the pilot separate or recount its plots consistently.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Stealth,node distance=0.6cm,
  box/.style={draw=bl,fill=bl!8,rounded corners,text width=3.6cm,align=center,minimum height=0.8cm,font=\small}]
\node[box] (a) {Try a few plots};
\node[box,below=of a] (b) {Measure time and\\variation in counts};
\node[box,below=of b] (c) {Agree plot size,\\effort and protocol};
\node[box,below=of c] (d) {Select the main sample};
\draw[->,thick] (a)--(b);\draw[->,thick] (b)--(c);\draw[->,thick] (c)--(d);
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 8. Navigate to the selected plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Take the plot list, offline map/GPS, compass, tape, markers and recording sheet.

\vspace{1em}

- Confirm the plot ID and location before counting.
- Use measured distances to mark corners; GPS alone may be too imprecise for a 10 m plot.
- Keep the selected location even if nearby trees look more interesting.
- If access fails, record the reason and follow an agreed revisit/replacement rule.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=Stealth]
\sampleplots\surveygrid\plotnumbers
\draw[bl,->,very thick] (-0.25,-0.4)--(0.5,0.5)--(1.5,2.5)--(3.5,2.5)--(3.5,4.5)--(0.5,3.5);
\fill[rd] (4.5,1.5) circle (0.12);
\node[font=\scriptsize,text=rd,align=center,fill=white] at (3.9,0.65) {Nearby trees do not\\change the plot list};
\node[font=\small] at (2.5,-0.8) {Choose the route after the plots};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 9. Count every eligible tree once

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Use the same search and counting rules in every plot.

\vspace{1em}

- One person searches; another records and checks boundaries.
- Mark or track counted trees to prevent double counting.
- Record the agreed unit.
- Recheck a subset of plots independently for missed trees.

\vspace{1em}

\alert{Complete detection is important} If eligible trees are being missed, improve the search protocol before continuing.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\sampleplots\surveygrid\sampletrees
\foreach \x/\y/\n in {3/4/2,0/3/2,1/2/1,3/2/1,0/0/0}{\node[anchor=north east,font=\scriptsize,text=bl] at (\x+0.98,\y+0.98) {\n};}
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-0.65) {Six trees counted in five plots\\White plots have not been surveyed};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 10. Record zeros and check the sheet each day

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Use **one row per plot**, including completed plots with no trees.

\vspace{1em}

- Record ID, coordinates, date, observers, area and count.
- Add habitat, completion status and access/protocol notes.
- Use 0 only after a complete search finds no eligible trees.
- Check missing IDs, duplicate rows and unusual counts before leaving the area.

\vspace{1em}

Save the original sheet and a digital backup. Keep counts for individual plots, not just the grand total.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.78cm,y=0.66cm]
\fill[bl!15] (0,5) rectangle (5,6);
\draw[gray] (0,0) rectangle (5,6);
\foreach \y in {1,...,5}{\draw[gray!65] (0,\y)--(5,\y);}
\draw[gray!65] (1.2,0)--(1.2,6);\draw[gray!65] (2.6,0)--(2.6,6);
\node[font=\small] at (0.6,5.5) {ID};\node[font=\small] at (1.9,5.5) {Count};\node[font=\small] at (3.8,5.5) {Status};
\foreach \id/\count/\y in {4/2/4.5,6/2/3.5,12/1/2.5,14/1/1.5,21/0/0.5}{
\node[font=\small] at (0.6,\y) {\id};\node[font=\small] at (1.9,\y) {\count};\node[font=\small] at (3.8,\y) {Complete};}
\draw[rd,thick] (1.9,0.5) ellipse (0.48 and 0.36);
\node[font=\small,text=rd] at (2.5,-0.7) {Zero is a valid observation};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::
::::

## 11. Estimate abundance: simple random

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Option A:** five plots sampled from 25 equal-area plots.

\vspace{1em}

Mean count per plot:
$$\bar y=\frac{2+2+1+1+0}{5}=1.2$$
$$\hat N=1.2\times25=\alert{30\ \text{trees}}$$

- Six trees counted in five plots.
- Each sampled plot represents $25/5=5$ plots.
- Include the zero count.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

\surveygrid\countplotnumbers

\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-0.85) {Blue numbers: observed counts\\Grey numbers: plot IDs};

## 11. Estimate abundance: stratified random

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Option B:** randomly sampled \textcolor{red}{6} of \textcolor{red}{15} woodland plots and \textcolor{blue}{4} of \textcolor{blue}{10} open-slope plots.

\vspace{1em}

Woodland: counts **1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1**.
$$\hat N_W=\frac{7}{6}\times15=17.5$$

Open slope: counts **1, 1, 0, 5**.
$$\hat N_O=\frac{7}{4}\times10=17.5$$

Add the two estimated totals:
$$\hat N=17.5+17.5=\alert{35\ \text{trees}}$$

## 11. Estimate abundance: systematic

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Option C:** nine plots on a grid with a random start.

\vspace{1em}

Ten trees counted in nine plots:
$$\bar y=\frac{10}{9}\approx1.11$$
$$\hat N=\frac{10}{9}\times25
\approx\alert{28\ \text{trees}}$$

\vspace{1em}

- Same calculation as for simple random sampling.
- Each sampled plot represents $25/9\approx2.8$ plots.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
\fill[bl!14] (0,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (2,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (2,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (4,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (4,4) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (0,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (2,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (2,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (4,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (4,2) rectangle +(1,1);
\fill[bl!14] (0,0) rectangle +(1,1);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,0) rectangle +(1,1);

## 12. Report uncertainty: simple random

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}

\footnotesize

```{r practical-ci-srs, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
library(survey)
srs <- data.frame(
  count = c(2, 2, 1, 1, 0),
  M = 25, w = 25/5)
d_srs <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
  weights = ~w, fpc = ~M, data = srs)
fit_srs <- svytotal(~count, d_srs)
coef(fit_srs)
confint(fit_srs, df = degf(d_srs))
```

\vspace{1em}
\footnotesize

`M` counts available plots; `w` is the number of plots each sampled plot represents. `fpc` accounts for sampling without replacement.

\vspace{1em}
\normalsize

**30 trees; approximate 95% CI: 7--53.**
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.065cm,y=0.85cm]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(62,0);
\foreach \x in {0,15,30,45,60}{\draw (\x,0.08)--(\x,-0.08) node[below,font=\scriptsize]{\x};}
\draw[bl,very thick] (6.770594,1.3)--(53.229406,1.3);
\draw[bl,thick] (6.770594,1.05)--(6.770594,1.55);
\draw[bl,thick] (53.229406,1.05)--(53.229406,1.55);
\fill[bl] (30,1.3) circle (2pt);
\node[above,font=\small] at (30,1.65) {Estimate: 30};

\end{tikzpicture}

## 12. Report uncertainty: stratified random

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
\footnotesize

```{r practical-ci-stratified, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
strat <- data.frame(
  count = c(1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,0,5),
  habitat = c("W","W","W","W","W","W",
              "O","O","O","O"),
  M = c(15,15,15,15,15,15,10,10,10,10),
  Msmp = c(6,6,6,6,6,6,4,4,4,4))
strat$w <- strat$M / strat$Msmp
d_strat <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
  strata = ~habitat, weights = ~w,
  fpc = ~M, data = strat)
fit_strat <- svytotal(~count, d_strat)
coef(fit_strat)
confint(fit_strat, df = degf(d_strat))
```

\vspace{1em}
\footnotesize

Tell R which counts belong to woodland (**W**) and open slope (**O**). `M` is the number of available plots **in each habitat**. R combines the two habitat totals and their uncertainty.

\vspace{1em}
\normalsize

**35 trees; approximate 95% CI: 15--55.**
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.065cm,y=0.85cm]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(62,0);
\foreach \x in {0,15,30,45,60}{\draw (\x,0.08)--(\x,-0.08) node[below,font=\scriptsize]{\x};}
\draw[bl,very thick] (14.6993,1.3)--(55.3007,1.3);
\draw[bl,thick] (14.6993,1.05)--(14.6993,1.55);
\draw[bl,thick] (55.3007,1.05)--(55.3007,1.55);
\fill[bl] (35,1.3) circle (2pt);
\node[above,font=\small] at (30,1.65) {Estimate: 35};
\node[font=\small] at (30,2.7) {Approximate 95\% CI};
\node[font=\small] at (30,-0.8) {Juniper trees in the patch};
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center,text width=3.7cm] at (30,-2.0) {Keep habitat labels and calculate uncertainty within each habitat before combining.};
\end{tikzpicture}
:::

## 12. Report uncertainty: systematic (approximation)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}

\footnotesize

```{r practical-ci-systematic, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
systematic <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 3, 5, 11, 13, 15, 21, 23, 25),
  count = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 3, 1),
  M = 25, w = 25/9)
d_sys <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
  weights = ~w, fpc = ~M,
  data = systematic)
fit_sys <- svytotal(~count, d_sys)
coef(fit_sys)
confint(fit_sys, df = degf(d_sys))
```

\footnotesize

This is an **approximation** assuming simple random sampling; it does not account for the dependence among plots on a systematic grid.

\vspace{1em}

**28 trees; approximate 95% CI: 16--40.**

:::
